title: Interpenetration
hookLine: Huayan: each thing contains all things, without blocking each other

cards: A lamp is already burning in the corner of the room. Someone comes in and lights a second one on the other side. The room gets brighter.
But notice what doesn't happen. The second light doesn't shove the first one out of the way. There's no line down the middle where one lamp's light stops and the other's starts.
Both lights fill the whole room, all of it, at the same time, and each is still its own flame. A school of Buddhist teachers in China said the whole world is built a little like that room.
Their word for it is interpenetration.

teach.b: Huayan teaches that each thing contains all things, and is contained in all things, and that they don't get in each other's way. The school's word for that last part is wu'ai: without obstruction.
Take it a step at a time. Huayan teachers spoke of the deep nature of things, which they called principle, and of particular things, which they called events. A cup is an event.
Its emptiness, the way it depends on everything else, is principle.

teach.h: PRINCIPLE AND EVENT, NOT IN THE WAY.
teach.b: Between principle and event, they said, there is no obstruction: the cup's emptiness isn't hiding behind the cup. It's right there in it. Then the bold step.

teach.h: EVENT AND EVENT, NOT IN THE WAY.
teach.b: Between one event and another there's no obstruction either. Not just the cup and its nature, but the cup and the table, the cup and the potter, the cup and the person drinking.
Each one holds the others, the way each lamp's light holds the room and the other light too. That is interpenetration. And it isn't everything blurring into one.
The second lamp is still the second lamp; blow it out, and the first keeps shining. Huayan insists on both halves: each thing is fully itself, in its own place, and each thing holds the whole.
Not a soup where everything melts, but a room full of distinct lights, none crowding the others out.
On an ordinary day, it's a hard and generous way to look at people: each person whole in their own right, and each one carrying everybody else.

how: Huayan Buddhists contemplate the interpenetration of principle and event, and of each event with every other, drawing on the Flower Garland Sutra and the commentaries of masters such as Fazang and Chengguan.

o: each thing holds all things, with nothing blocking another
the way water slowly soaks into stone over time
all things melting together into one formless soup

p: a particular thing, like a cup

s: interpenetration means everything melts into one
each thing stays fully itself, in its own place, and still holds the whole.
Huayan says event and event don't obstruct each other
not only a cup and its nature, but the cup and the table and the potter.
in Huayan, a thing's emptiness hides behind it
between principle and event there's no obstruction. it's right there in the thing.

games.q: you light a second lamp in a room already lit. Huayan asks: what happens to the first lamp's light?
o: it gets pushed into one corner.
it vanishes into the new light.
both fill the whole room, each still itself.
games.why: neither crowds the other out. that picture of distinct things not blocking each other is what Huayan calls without obstruction.

practice: Find a place where two things meet, your hand resting on your knee, your feet on the floor, and stay with that one meeting. Is the hand touching the knee, or the knee touching the hand?
Notice that both are happening, neither pushing the other out, each staying itself and each changed by the other.

wordCard.voice: Interpenetration. Huayan's teaching that each thing holds all things and is held by them, with nothing blocking anything else. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese shishi wu'ai: event and event without obstruction, Huayan's boldest step.

carryVoice: Your line: without obstruction. Two lamps, one room, and neither one crowding the other out. Until tomorrow.
